Sleep quality improved (effect size 0.14, P < 0.05), total sleep time increased (mean 25.2 minutes, P < 0.001), and the number of night time awakenings decreased (0.63, P < 0.001) with sedative use compared with placebo." Methods: "total sleep time (total amount of time participants perceive that they have slept, measured in minutes)... Ratings were made by patients and not an observer." claims.safe_wording: In short trials in people aged 60 and over, sleeping tablets added about 25 minutes of sleep a night on average, as reported by the people taking them, and about one fewer waking every two nights (0.63 fewer wakings a night).

The rate of hyponatremia was 146 per 1,000 person-years for adults prescribed desmopressin compared to 11 per 1,000 person-years for adults prescribed oxybutynin, corresponding to a 13-fold higher rate (HR 13.19; 95% CI 6.69, 26.01; p < 0.01)." ... candidates.reason: All essential claims verified in the Glass 2005 full text: 25.2 minutes self-reported total sleep time and 0.63 fewer awakenings (trials of at least 5 nights, up to 9 weeks, published 1966 to 2003); NNT 13 (sleep quality; 4 trials, 1,072 people, specific drugs; CI 6.7 to 62.9) and NNH 6 (any adverse event; 16 trials, 2,220 people), with the authors' own caveat that the ratio is a rough indicator; cognitive events and daytime fatigue more common. Beers 2023 Table 2 text verified (avoid benzodiazepines and Z-drugs, 'minimal improvement in sleep latency and duration'). CBT-I first line verified in ACP 2016 and European 2023 guidelines; the European guideline allows short-term tablets (4 weeks or less), consistent with the candidate's position. Required changes to wording: say 'self-reported' and 'in short trials'; do not show 'unsteadiness' or falls as a Glass finding (P>0.05); do not convert odds ratios; label the NNT and NNH icon arrays as coming from different trials and outcomes; optionally note the publication-bias-adjusted estimate of 15 minutes. Berry 2013 (Z-drugs and hip fracture in US care homes) is optional and must be worded as an association.

The teatime loop diuretic example is contradicted by evidence: nocturia guidance advises taking diuretics no later than mid to late afternoon, and a randomised trial found furosemide taken about 6 hours before bed reduced night-time urination. The Parkinson's element has no openable source (NICE NG71 not accessible) and is dropped. Donepezil morning dosing rests on reviews and an 8-patient case series (supported with qualification); the steroid single-morning-dose advice rests on expert guidance (supported with qualification). Hospital sleep disturbers (noise, devices, pain, toilet visits) and the sedative trade-off in people over 60 are well supported.
candidates.revised_angle: Two lists for the 2am call. Tonight: ask about pain, a full bladder, noise and equipment, the disturbances inpatients report most (Wesselius 2018), before reaching for a sedative, which in people over 60 adds only about 25 minutes of self-reported sleep with more confusion and daytime tiredness (Glass 2005). Tomorrow, for the day team: review dose times. Is a steroid given later than the morning (expert advice favours a single morning dose)? Is donepezil given at night in someone with sleeplessness or vivid dreams (reviews suggest morning dosing may help)? Is a diuretic given in the evening (guidance: no later than mid to late afternoon)? Do not name a teatime loop diuretic as a culprit, and leave out Parkinson's medicines.

candidates.reason: Both Quebec trials verified from PubMed abstracts: EMPOWER 27% versus 5% stopped at 6 months (risk difference 23 points, NNT 4; further 11% reduced dose; 62% of recipients raised it themselves); D-PRESCRIBE sedative-hypnotic subgroup 63/146 (43.2%) versus 14/155 (9.0%), with 29 of 77 tapering reporting withdrawal symptoms and no adverse events needing hospital care. The EMPOWER abstract does not say the booklet was posted, so say 'given'. Outcomes were pharmacy refill records, not confirmed abstinence.
